title: How do you get through the maths in a case without mistakes?
description: Numbers turn opinions into evidence. Errors under pressure are the most common confidence killer. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Get through case maths without mistakes by stating your approach before any arithmetic, calculating out loud with units attached, sanity-checking every result, and then saying what the number means for the client. The sums themselves are usually simple. What makes them hard is doing them with someone watching, and that is exactly what this routine is for.
body:
Stage 7 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why the maths matters

Numbers turn opinions into evidence. "Delivery is hurting profit" is a guess; "delivery adds $0.45 per order instead of $4.50" is a finding. Slips under pressure are also a common confidence killer, and you will usually work without a calculator: McKinsey's sample cases note that calculators are not allowed and that you can write calculations out on paper.

The four-step routine

1. Approach before arithmetic

Write down what you are being asked. Then state the formula and check it before you touch a number. McKinsey's own sample-case tips say the same: take time to plan how to approach the calculation, then describe your approach and talk the interviewer through it.

"My approach: units sold × contribution per unit, minus the fixed launch cost. Does that make sense before I run the numbers?"

Agreement on the approach means a small arithmetic slip costs you little, because the interviewer can see your logic is right.

2. Calculate out loud, with units

Say each step as you write it, and keep the unit attached: "$20 per part", "parts per year". Bain's guidance asks candidates to share their reasoning and calculations, even when unsure. Talking through the steps also lets the interviewer catch a slip early. For big numbers, count zeros carefully or switch to millions and thousands. The tricks are in how to multiply big numbers without losing the zeros.

3. Sanity-check the result

After every result, check the order of magnitude out loud. Compare it with something you already know: the market size, last year's revenue, the client's target.

"Quick sanity check: 2M units at $50 is $100M, which is 20% of a $500M market. Plausible for a market leader."

Round sensibly, and say so. Rounding 5.5 to 5 is a 9% error; rounding it to 6 is about 9% the other way. If precision matters for the decision, keep the decimal.

4. Say the so-what

A number on its own earns little. Finish with what it means: "...which is $100M, half the client's $200M target, so we need at least one more lever."

A worked example

A factory sells a part for $50, with $30 of variable cost per part. It is considering leasing new machinery for $2M a year. How many extra parts must it sell to cover the lease?

Approach: "Each extra part contributes price minus variable cost. Divide the lease by that contribution to get break-even volume."

Calculation: contribution per part = $50 − $30 = $20. Break-even = $2M ÷ $20 = 100,000 parts a year.

Sanity check: 100,000 × $20 = $2M. Correct.

So what: the maths gives a threshold, not a decision. Now ask the business questions. Can the factory sell another 100,000 parts at $50? Does it have the capacity? Does the lease replace another cost? If it expects to sell 120,000 extra parts, the lease adds 120,000 × $20 − $2M = $400k a year. More on this formula in break-even in one line.

Market sizing extras

For estimation questions, add three habits: give a rough guess first, say whether you will size it from the demand side or the supply side, and cross-check if there is time.

"Before I size it, my instinct says somewhere in the tens of thousands. Let me test that from the demand side: population, visits per person and the visits one dentist can handle."

The guess gives you something to sanity-check against. See how to answer a market sizing question for the full method.

Common mistakes

  • Calculating in silence. The interviewer cannot give credit for logic they cannot see.
  • Starting with numbers before the approach. One wrong formula wastes the whole calculation.
  • Dropping units. "100,000" of what, and per what period?
  • No sanity check. A result ten times too big is the classic slip, and a ten-second check catches it.
  • Leaving the number hanging. Always compare it with the goal.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. You are asked for the profit impact of a new product line. What do you say before any numbers?

Show a strong answer

"My approach: units sold × contribution per unit, minus the fixed launch cost. Does that make sense before I run the numbers?"

Why it works: Agreement on the approach protects you from wasted work.

2. You have calculated $100M of revenue from 2M units at $50. Finish the calculation properly.

Show a strong answer

"Quick sanity check: that's 20% of a $500M market, which seems plausible for a market leader. So about $100M, which I'd now compare with the client's target."

Why it works: A sanity check, then the so-what.

3. A subscription costs $15 a month and the client expects 40,000 subscribers. Annual revenue?

Show a strong answer

"$15 × 12 months = $180 a year per subscriber. $180 × 40,000 = $7.2M a year. Sanity check: $15 × 40,000 is $600k a month, and twelve of those is $7.2M. Consistent."

Why it works: The same answer reached two ways is the fastest check there is.

Where to practise next

Do five minutes of the maths drill daily; speed comes from reps. Keep the 20 formulas for case maths to hand, and read how to do case maths out loud for more worked examples. The next stage is answering "What else could the client do?".
